item.title: 10 Deadly Sins of a Beginning Product Manager
item.description:
This article was originally published on habr.com.

These «deadly sins» can serve as a self-assessment checklist for both beginner and more experienced managers.

So, here are the mistakes — and how to fix them.

1. Believing in multitasking

Every product manager faces enormous flows of information, including all manner of product development initiatives and ideas that no single person can possibly process within the time available. Stakeholders push their agendas, users complain, the calendar is packed with meetings, and the Product Backlog grows day by day.

item.title: Thinking Through Writing
item.description:
I came across a fascinating interview with Andrei Styskin (Director at Amazon, former CEO of the search division at Yandex), in which Andrei talks about some interesting aspects of Amazon’s internal culture — specifically, the «document-centric» approach to meetings and decision-making.

  1. Every meeting is a collaborative effort in which participants work together on a pre-prepared document focused on a specific problem. Part of the time (10 to 20 minutes) is spent reading the document independently; the rest is used for discussion and commentary. If open questions remain after the meeting, another meeting is scheduled in the same format. The process continues until the requirements are unambiguously defined and agreed upon by all stakeholders.
  2. Requirements for any product or feature are developed using the «Working Backwards» method, through writing two documents: a «Press Release» and a «FAQ.» The product manager writes a press release long before the release date, thereby forming a vision of the ideal launch outcome — a north star that the product team can orient toward throughout development.
  3. All decisions are made through document reviews, not through informal verbal conversations in meetings or by the coffee machine, as so often happens in most workplaces.

Reflecting on my time at Yandex (a great company, though not quite global in scale — for comparison, in 2024 Yandex’s market cap was $10 billion, while Amazon’s was $2 trillion), I can say that the company’s internal culture encourages employees to express their thinking in writing: at Yandex, it’s standard practice to maintain detailed wiki documentation, write thorough task descriptions in the issue tracker, discuss questions in comments, and keep internal blogs — both public and anonymous. The more senior an employee’s position, the more persuasively and concisely they tend to write and communicate their ideas.

item.title: On the Certified Scrum Product Owner Certification
item.description:
In his book Empowered: Ordinary People, Extraordinary Products, Marty Cagan recommends that aspiring product managers get CSPO-certified early in their careers. I want to share what you can actually expect from this training and certification — beyond just another achievement to add to your profile (and a fairly pricey one at that).

The training runs for two full days. The first day covers agile and scrum fundamentals through group exercises, with a brief overview of other product development methodologies. For anyone just entering the profession, this day is genuinely valuable — it builds a deeper, more intentional understanding of scrum. That knowledge serves as a useful baseline for evaluating and comparing the processes at your own company or within your product.

More experienced product managers will find the first day helpful for formalizing and structuring what they already know. Most of us work directly with development teams, and a fresh perspective can bring new energy and creative thinking to those relationships.
